item.title: Living With CSBD: What Treatment Can Help?
item.description:
Sex Addiction

Living With CSBD: What Treatment Can Help?

An overview of evidence-based support for compulsive sexual behavior disorder

Posted June 10, 2026

Key points
  • CSBD involves loss of control over sexual behavior, leading to distress and impairment.
  • ICD-11 recognition has improved diagnostic clarity and clinical legitimacy of CSBD.
  • CBT is the most commonly used treatment approach for CSBD, although no gold standard exists.
  • Effective support is possible even without a formal diagnosis, depending on individual needs.

This post was written by Professor Dr. Stephanie Antons from the University of Siegen, an expert on compulsive sexual behavior disorder (CSBD) and problematic usage of the Internet. Through her research, she investigates the psychological mechanisms underlying CSBD and evidence-based approaches to its treatment.

The recognition of CSBD as a clinical entity in the 11th edition of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), an international manual published by the World Health Organization, has been an important step in bringing greater clarity to a previously controversial and inconsistently defined condition. It has helped establish CSBD as a legitimate mental health concern that can be systematically studied and treated.

Individuals with compulsive sexual behavior disorder (CSBD) experience a persistent pattern of failure to control intense, repetitive sexual impulses or urges, leading to repetitive sexual behavior that results in significant distress or impairment in daily life: for example, neglecting health, work, or relationships (see previous blog post). Strong sexual urges alone are not sufficient for a diagnosis of CSBD. Clinically relevant distress or functional impairment that cannot be explained solely by moral incongruence is a key diagnostic criterion.

Although evidence-based research on treatments for CSBD is still in its early stages, systematic reviews of the international literature (Antons et al., 2022; Briken et al., 2024) as well as a recent German S1 treatment guideline (Stark et al., 2025) provide valuable insights into which interventions appear most promising and where important gaps in the evidence remain.

The following sections summarize the key findings from these sources.

Diagnosis as a first step to treatment

If you experience symptoms of CSBD, the first step is usually to consult a qualified professional (such as a psychotherapist, psychiatrist, or sexual health specialist) who can conduct a comprehensive assessment. Receiving an accurate diagnosis is important because it helps ensure that treatment is appropriately tailored to the underlying mechanisms driving the symptoms.

For example, in some cases, distress may be primarily driven by moral incongruence rather than a loss of behavioral control (see previous blog post). In such cases, treatment approaches that explicitly address these value conflicts may be particularly relevant. A thorough assessment is also essential because it helps identify co-occurring conditions (such as depression, anxiety disorders, or substance use problems) that often require concurrent treatment.

In addition, a formal diagnosis can improve access to care, including the likelihood of insurance coverage in many healthcare systems. Since the inclusion of CSBD in the ICD-11, recognition of the condition within healthcare settings has increased, although access to specialized treatment remains variable.

Psychological treatment approaches

Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is currently the most widely used and best-supported psychotherapeutic approach for CSBD. While there is still no universally established “gold standard” treatment, CBT-based interventions are most commonly recommended in clinical practice.

CBT protocols typically include several core components, such as psychoeducation (understanding the mechanisms of the disorder), self-regulation and urge management strategies (learning to identify and respond differently to triggers), mindfulness-based techniques (increasing awareness of thoughts, emotions, and urges), and relapse prevention (developing long-term strategies to maintain behavioral change).

CBT can be delivered individually or in groups, and treatment goals are often tailored to the individual. While some individuals may aim for complete abstinence from specific behaviors (such as problematic pornography use), others may focus on regaining control and establishing a healthier, more satisfying sexual life without compulsive patterns.

Alternative and complementary approaches

Other therapeutic approaches, such as acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), may also be helpful, particularly for individuals who experience strong moral incongruence or internal conflict. ACT focuses on increasing psychological flexibility and supporting behavior that aligns with personal values.

In addition, couples therapy can be an important complementary approach, especially when CSBD is associated with significant relationship distress or when couples aim to rebuild trust and work toward long-term intimacy goals.

Online self-help programs and digital interventions can also provide accessible support, particularly when face-to-face therapy is not readily available.

Pharmacological options

Pharmacological treatment options for CSBD remain limited, and the current evidence base is still developing. While medication alone is not considered a first-line treatment, some pharmacological approaches have been explored as adjunctive options, particularly in moderate to severe cases or when psychotherapy alone is insufficient.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), commonly used for depression and anxiety disorders, may help reduce the intensity of intrusive sexual thoughts and support the treatment of co-occurring mood symptoms. Opioid antagonists, such as naltrexone, have also been investigated for their potential to reduce reward-related reinforcement of compulsive behaviors. However, these treatments are typically considered off-label and should be carefully evaluated on an individual basis.

What if there is no formal diagnosis?

Even in the absence of a formal diagnosis, individuals who experience distress related to their sexual behavior can still benefit from professional support. Many therapeutic approaches focus on symptom reduction, emotional regulation, and improving overall quality of life—regardless of whether diagnostic criteria are fully met.
